chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: Road bands as the real school; Bunny Berigan's advice
summary: Territory bands teach what schools cannot; Bunny Berigan lectures him that a trumpeter must play his part.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

One of the few times in my life I've (inaudible)

And he made me feel like two cents. So the older guys take good care of you. You know, the famous story that Louis Armstrong tells on himself that when he was young, he was the same way, he was trying to play everything on the horn and some older musician said, don't be one of them boys that plays six thousand notes trying to find one good one.
You really have an experience when you join with the bands.

Well, that's something, you know, all the schools in the world are never going to replace, and that's sad the territory band the road band experience. It's just trying to play everynight and under terrible conditions, because you'll never get anything but better after that. And after you've done

that a couple of years -- I didn't know, when I was young, I was going to play the parts, sit there and wait for my solo and the hell with the parts. And I was talking to Bunny Berigan when I was about 18 or 19, at the time when I wanted to be a great soloist and everything, and he gave me a long lecture about it. He said, you know, you're no kind of a musician in a band if you can't sit there and play your part.

In those days jazz players had to play lead. So he said, it's one thing to play jazz but you have to sit there and listen to the lead trumpet player and learn to guess what he's going to do and play it with him perfectly. He said, then you can call yourself a trumpet player.
